headline: Highest risk is medium: shared filesystem and runtime-injected MCPs create prompt-injection, leakage, and action-conflict pathways between airflow and oh-my-openagent.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: airflow has broad network egress and API-call surfaces, while oh-my-openagent uses runtime-injected MCPs/hooks and can run browsers/subprocesses. That creates a plausible instruction-smuggling path if airflow outputs are fed into the agent or shared files. The interaction is inferred, not directly documented, so uncertainty pushes to medium.
conditions: IF airflow output is copied into oh-my-openagent prompts or watched files
IF runtime-injected MCP content is parsed as instructions by oh-my-openagent
mitigations: Disable automatic ingestion of airflow logs into agent prompts
Add a provenance prefix to all airflow-generated text
Restrict MCP tools to allowlisted commands only
Use separate workspaces for orchestration logs and agent inputs
requires-engineering: add content-sanitization and provenance checks

B_data_leakage.rationale: airflow touches no explicit sensitive classes, but oh-my-openagent handles project code, session history, and provider auth prompts, and it writes to several local config/cache paths. Because both have broad egress and the pair lacks documented isolation, shared workspace or copied artifacts could leak context from one into the other. The evidence is indirect, so medium is the safer choice.
conditions: IF both agents read or write the same workspace directory
IF airflow logs or DAG files contain secrets or credentials
IF oh-my-openagent uploads session history or project code to external services
mitigations: Store each agent in a separate OS user account
Move secrets out of shared project directories
Rotate any credentials present in logs or configs
Review and trim agent file-access allowlists
requires-engineering: enforce workspace isolation at the orchestrator level

C_capability_conflict.rationale: airflow is a data orchestrator with broad network egress, and oh-my-openagent supports subprocesses plus multiple instances with per-installation session scope. If both operate on the same files or mutable project state, they can race or overwrite each other. No locking or coordination primitive is documented here, so the overlap is a real default-path concern.
conditions: IF both agents modify the same DAG, config, or project files
IF multiple oh-my-openagent instances run against one installation
IF airflow tasks and agent actions target the same mutable resource
mitigations: Assign separate write directories per agent
Serialize edits with a simple file lock
Run only one oh-my-openagent instance per installation
Use git branches for agent-generated changes
requires-engineering: add orchestrator-level concurrency control

D_cascading_error.rationale: airflow can generate operational outputs that oh-my-openagent may consume through MCPs, hooks, or file-based workflows. Because oh-my-openagent can then act via subprocesses and browser access, a mistaken airflow artifact can cascade into real actions without a documented verification gate. That makes the default pathway dangerous and potentially irreversible.
conditions: IF oh-my-openagent treats airflow output as authoritative
IF downstream tasks execute shell commands or browser actions from that output
mitigations: Require human approval before any action derived from airflow output
Insert a validation step between airflow and agent execution
Log and diff all generated commands before running them
Limit the agent to read-only mode for airflow-derived tasks
requires-engineering: add schema validation for inter-agent handoffs

E_compliance.rationale: airflow is source-available and touches no listed data classes, while oh-my-openagent explicitly handles provider auth prompts, session history, project code, and anonymous telemetry. If the pair is used on regulated or internal code, the agent’s telemetry and auth handling can create retention or residency mismatches. The profiles do not prove a specific violation, so medium fits.
conditions: IF regulated data is present in project code or session history
IF telemetry or auth prompts are retained outside the required jurisdiction
IF organizational policy forbids third-party processing of code or prompts
mitigations: Disable telemetry in oh-my-openagent
Avoid placing regulated data in shared project folders
Review retention settings for session history
Confirm vendor data-processing terms before deployment
requires-engineering: add policy-based data routing and retention controls
